name: Nikhil Khan

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for seeing me, Nikhil. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything here is confidential. Can you tell me about a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work in policy servicing at an old life insurance company in the business park off the ring road. People ring or write in to change an address, add a new beneficiary after a wedding, or cash in an old policy, and I process it. A lot of it is policies from the nineties, paper files scanned badly, so you have to squint. I've been there six years and I know where all the bodies are buried, so to speak.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like that it's orderly. A form comes in, I check the signature and the ID, I update the system, done. I don't like change for the sake of it; we got a new screen layout last year and it took me three months to stop swearing at it. I don't use any of those AI chat things, not at work, not at home. What wears me out is the death claims, honestly, talking to widows about forms.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, let's get on with the job. I'd probably say it to the lads at cricket on Saturday, that the computers still can't read a 1997 signature. I don't post online about work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it's not all calm. Half my day is changing addresses on life policies people bought in the nineties. If a computer does that half, I'd better be very good at the other half. And we merged with another life insurer last year, so there's already talk of restructuring.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing what I do, careful and steady. Sana and I would keep putting 400 a month into the wedding fund, we need about 8,000 by next August. I'd keep my head down and make sure my error rate stays the lowest on the team.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit uneasy. Not because of AI so much as the merger.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Tell me about the merger. What's the worry?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: There are two servicing teams now doing the same work in two buildings. Someone in head office will notice that eventually. I'd guess they close one office, and I don't know which.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If they closed yours, what would you do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Look for the same job at another insurer; there are a few in the city. The commute would be worse, maybe an hour each way. I'd take it rather than learn something completely new.

do: Keep working **carefully** and keep the lowest error rate on the team.
Keep saving **400 a month** with Sana for the wedding.
Look at **other insurers** in the city if his office closed.
feel: **Uneasy**, more about the **merger** than about AI.

steps.text: Keep the lowest error rate on the policy servicing team
Save 400 a month with Sana for the wedding

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's business; companies will always cut costs where they can. I'd tell people at work to make sure they're useful. Online, nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be worried. My whole job is checking forms and writing letters, which is that list on the card. I've never typed a question into a chatbot in my life, and I'm the kind of clerk that gets cut first in a world like that. With the merger on top, I'd say there's a real chance I'm gone in two years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd cut back now: fewer takeaways, no new phone, and I'd cancel the cricket club's tour this summer, about 600 saved. I'd talk to Sana about trimming the wedding guest list from 200 to 120. I'd wait to see who they keep before I do any courses, because I don't want to pay for the wrong one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Like waiting for exam results you know went badly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd cut the guest list. How would that conversation go?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Badly, at first. Sana's mum has already told half the family. But Sana's sensible, she works in a pharmacy and sees prices going up. I'd tell Sana a smaller wedding beats starting married life with a loan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you wouldn't learn the tools. If your manager asked you to, would you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If my manager made it part of the job, I'd do it, I'm not stupid. I just wouldn't volunteer. I'd learn exactly enough to keep my seat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say nobody's ready for this and I'm not going to pretend I am. I'd tell my mates to hold on to their cash. I'd keep it off the internet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd be out of work within two years, no question. Servicing life policies is pure paperwork. Our wedding is booked for next August. In that world I'd be ringing the venue to ask how much deposit we lose if we cancel.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd move the wedding to a small family do and put the rest of the fund, about 6,000, into savings. I'd stop all spending that isn't rent, food and the car. Once it arrives, I'd go and ask my uncle about work at his tyre and exhaust garage, because hands-on jobs would have about three years before robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared. Proper scared, the kind where you check your bank app at night.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your parents say?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My dad would say he told me to learn a trade. He was a bus driver for thirty years and always said offices aren't safe. I used to laugh at that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd go to your uncle's garage. Would you actually do it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If my job was gone and the rent was due, yes. I'd hate it at first. I don't even like changing my own tyres.

steps.text: Shrink the wedding to a small family do

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's time to sort it, so the government and companies should sort it. I'd tell colleagues to get a backup plan. I wouldn't say much more than that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years means my job goes, just a bit later. My uncle's tyre garage always needs a hand. I never wanted to smell of rubber for a living, but five years of warning would change my mind. The garage would be safe until about 2034, which is a while.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my job and keep the wedding as planned, maybe a bit smaller. In the second or third year, I'd start working Saturdays at the garage to learn the basics, which means giving up cricket. I'd keep saving 300 a month so we have six months by the time it comes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, but less sick about it. There's a ladder to climb down instead of a cliff.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Giving up cricket sounds like a big thing for you.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It is, I've played since I was twelve. But Saturdays at the garage would be practice for something real. I could still play the odd Sunday match.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about Sana? How does she fit into this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sana's pharmacy job is more hands-on than mine, so she'd probably last longer. We'd keep her wage for the mortgage and mine for everything else. That's the plan we'd make, anyway.

S3.quote: My uncle's tyre garage always needs a hand. I never wanted to smell of rubber for a living, but five years of warning would change my mind.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long time and lots could change. I'd tell people not to panic. Honestly I'd probably not talk about it much.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, ten years is long enough that I'd probably leave it too late. People like me need a deadline before we move. I'd tell myself I'll start next year, every year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get married, carry on at work and save as normal, about 200 a month after the wedding. I'd probably think about the garage around year five or six, not before. I'd wait and see what my colleagues do first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fine, mostly. A small itch at the back of my head.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd leave it too late. Would anything stop that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If Sana pushed me, maybe. Or if someone at work I respect left for a new job and it worked out. I follow people, I don't lead.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the itch feel like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Like a dentist appointment I keep putting off. It's not urgent, until one day it is.

I'd tell people **not to panic** and wouldn't talk about it much.
think: Ten years means he'd probably **leave it too late**.
People like him need a **deadline** before they move, and ten years isn't one.
do: Get married and **save 200 a month** after the wedding.
Look at **garage work** around year five or six.
**Wait** to see what colleagues do first.

S4.quote: Ten years is long enough that I'd probably leave it too late. People like me need a deadline before we move.
fieldNote: He knows his **procrastination** and names it honestly.

steps.text: Get married next August as planned

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because it lands right on top of our wedding and our first years together. Nobody at a life insurer ever got fired for being careful. I just never imagined careful would stop being enough. What would help is proper notice from the company and paid time off to learn a trade, so I'm not doing it on Saturdays.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe about the customers. Lots of our policyholders are old and they ring because they want a person. I don't know who they'll talk to.

headlineQuote: Nobody at a life insurer ever got fired for being careful. I just never imagined careful would stop being enough.
portrait: Nikhil, 27, services **life insurance policies** and is saving with Sana for a wedding next August.
He never uses AI and prefers **order and routine** over change.
He sees cuts as **business**, not anyone's fault.
Under pressure he **shrinks spending** and leans on his uncle's tyre garage.
He admits that with ten years he'd **leave it too late**.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because it lands on top of the **wedding** and first married years.
whatWouldHelp: **Paid time off** to learn a trade.
